case_against: "Mirror" tariffs are taxes paid by Americans, not by foreign countries. Federal Reserve Bank of New York economists found that nearly 90 percent of the cost of the 2025 tariffs fell on U.S. firms and consumers. Matching every country's tariffs also invites retaliation, as in 2018-2019, when trading partners hit U.S. farm exports and USDA paid about $25.7 billion to help farmers. The Supreme Court ruled in 2026 that the emergency law used for the 2025 "reciprocal" tariffs did not allow them.

harms.what: Pay higher prices on imported goods and on products made with imported parts.
Are the usual targets of retaliation and can lose overseas customers.

history.what: A farm-relief bill grew into broad tariff increases across the economy. Many countries adopted similar "beggar-thy-neighbor" policies, and U.S. exports to Europe fell from $2.3 billion in 1929 to $784 million in 1932. Historians debate how much the tariff itself deepened the Depression.
history.lesson: Tit-for-tat tariffs shrank trade for everyone. Starting in 1934, the U.S. turned to negotiated tariff cuts instead.

case_against: Fully cutting economic ties with China would raise costs for American families and businesses that rely on Chinese goods and parts, and would invite retaliation against U.S. exporters. After the U.S. raised tariffs on Chinese goods in 2018, China put tariffs on U.S. soybeans, and soybean exports to China fell 74 percent by value that year, according to the Congressional Research Service. USDA then paid farmers billions in aid. The administration itself has moved between tariff hikes and trade truces, showing how costly a full break would be.

harms.what: Lost sales when China targeted soybeans and other U.S. crops in past trade fights, and would face that risk again.
Would pay more for goods and parts that are hard to source elsewhere.

case_against: Tariffs high enough to block all Chinese goods would be paid mostly by Americans. Studies of the 2018 tariffs found they were fully passed on to U.S. prices, costing Americans about $1.4 billion a month in real income by the end of 2018. New York Fed economists found U.S. firms and consumers bore nearly 90 percent of the 2025 tariffs. China answered earlier U.S. tariffs with its own, raising them to 125 percent on U.S. goods in April 2025.

harms.what: Pay more for electronics, clothing, toys and other products when tariffs are passed on.
Face retaliation that closes off one of their largest markets.

history.what: Broad U.S. tariff increases were followed by similar moves abroad. World trade fell by about 66 percent between 1929 and 1934. Historians debate how much retaliation the tariff itself caused.
history.lesson: Very high tariffs and the responses they provoke can shrink trade sharply, hurting exporters along with importers.

case_against: Banning all Chinese social media apps would cut off platforms that tens of millions of Americans use to speak, work and stay in touch; TikTok alone had more than 170 million U.S. users. When the government tried in 2020 to restrict TikTok and WeChat by executive order, courts blocked those orders. Congress later chose a narrower law requiring a sale of TikTok, and a sale is what happened, showing a full ban was not necessary.

harms.what: Could lose a main way to talk with friends, family and communities, including people overseas.
Could lose audiences and income built on these platforms.

history.what: Executive orders 13942 and 13943 sought to restrict TikTok and WeChat. Court injunctions blocked them, and they were later replaced.
history.lesson: Sweeping app bans ran into legal limits; narrower, law-based approaches were used instead.

case_against: Broad visa cuts for Chinese students and researchers would push scientific talent to other countries. The Congressional Research Service notes that research security rules can slow scientific progress, which itself can hurt national and economic security, and cites scientists warning of a "chilling effect" on international collaboration. Targeted screening of real security risks is possible without shutting out a whole nationality, a point the chapter's free-trade author also makes.

harms.what: Could lose researchers and tuition, slowing work in science and engineering.
Could face suspicion and lost opportunities because of nationality rather than conduct.
